extracted.intended_audience: general readers; librarians, educators, students, and researchers interested in censorship and library policy
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive encyclopedic summary of book censorship in the United States, including definitions, historical background, types/forms of censorship, legal cases, institutional procedures, and common reasons books are challenged or removed. Useful as a reference for understanding how and why books are censored and how institutions and courts have responded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of book censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Book censorship is the act of restricting access to books, due to images, ideas, or information contained, because the individual or organization requesting censorship finds the content objectionable. It refers specifically to attempts to remove or curtail access to a work for a whole population – such as all the children at a school or all the patrons of a public library – and does not include an individual's decision that a book is not appropriate for themselves or their dependents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes population-level restrictions (institutional removal or limitation) rather than private choices; includes printed, electronic, audiobook, and curriculum materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of active censorship (Emily Knox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of 'active' censorship: Removal, Relocation, Restriction, and Redaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal: abolishing certain books from shelves; Relocation: moving books to harder-to-access locations (e.g., 'adults only' sections); Restriction: limiting access unless special permission is obtained; Redaction: striking through or covering sections of materials so they cannot be seen. These forms can be applied across bookstores, libraries, and schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration policies and due process
rubrics_metrics.description: Many libraries and educational institutions have 'reconsideration policies' that lay out how to file a challenge and what happens after one has been filed. These policies exist to make the challenge process transparent and consistent and to support due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically an administrator or a committee will consider the challenge and the text and make a determination; if the challenge is supported, the book may be removed. Policies aim to ensure transparency and consistent handling of challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'banned book'
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'banned book' is one that has been 'removed from a library, classroom, etc.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes outright removal from restrictions or relocation; removal from access constitutes being 'banned' in many discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling effect / passive censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Rise in book challenges can produce a 'chilling effect' leading to increased self-censorship ('passive censorship') by many institutions, often at the level of school districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may preemptively remove or avoid purchasing materials to forestall controversy, not necessarily through formal bans but by changing acquisition or display practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and legal standards (freedom to read)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom to read arguments cite the U.S. Constitution—particularly the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments—and legal precedent to limit censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have set boundaries on school boards and other actors removing books; legal tests and case law (e.g., Island Trees School District v. Pico) govern when removals violate the First Amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Island Trees School District v. Pico standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court ruled that 'Local school boards may not remove books from school library shelves simply because they dislike the ideas contained in those books' and that First Amendment limitations apply to the discretion of school boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School boards retain broad discretion to choose curriculum materials, but may not exercise library-removal discretion in a narrowly partisan or political manner; libraries are treated as institutions affording public access to discussion and ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between curriculum selection and library holdings
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have upheld that school boards may disallow certain texts in curricula while finding removal from libraries unconstitutional (e.g., Minarcini v. Strongsville: removal from curriculum allowed, removal from library unconstitutional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal treatment differs: selecting classroom materials (curriculum) involves pedagogical discretion; library collections are viewed as 'storehouses of knowledge' with stronger First Amendment protections against viewpoint-based removals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content-neutral vs content-based censorship (carceral context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content-neutral bans restrict literature for reasons unrelated to its content (e.g., not mailed from an approved bookseller, format restrictions); content-based bans reject books because of specific content (e.g., sexual explicitness, security threats, race, non-English languages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In prisons, 'approved-vendor' policies are common (a content-neutral restriction) while content-based bans are justified by officials on grounds of security, sexual content, or communication in non-English languages. Distinguishing the two is important for assessing the rationale and legality of restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved-vendor policy (prison mailrooms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many prison mailrooms require literature to be mailed through a publisher or approved vendor directly, even if the content is neutral and does not threaten security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PEN America found 84% of prison mailrooms followed approved-vendor policies; this is an example of a content-neutral administrative restriction that limits access regardless of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common top reasons for challenges (ALA / Office for Intellectual Freedom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Top cited reasons for challenging materials: the material was considered 'sexually explicit'; the material contained 'offensive language'; the material was 'unsuited to any age group'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These high-level reasons cover many specific complaints and are used by reporting organizations to categorize challenges; ALA reports many additional, more specific reasons (more than 20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trends in contemporary challenges (2021–2023)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent trends include bans/challenges targeting: books detailing sexual violence (framed as 'obscene'); LGBTQ+ books and instruction on sexual orientation or gender identity; particular focus on transgender narratives; backlash framed as 'Critical Race Theory'—books about race or characters of color labeled 'divisive'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These trends reflect thematic targeting and political framing that have driven a dramatic increase in challenges since 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexually explicit content as grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are challenged for sexual content including sexual education, rape, sexual assault, sexually explicit images or references; concern that such material might 'encourage children' or be 'unsuited to age group'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ground is often applied to both explicit depictions and, controversially, to any LGBTQ content even when non-sexual (e.g., depiction of same-sex relationships).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive language / profanity as grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of profanity and vulgar language (e.g., frequent use of the f-word) is a common reason for attempts to challenge or remove books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of 'offensive' is subjective; defenders often argue context and literary or social value outweighs profanity-based objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race-related grounds (racism, racial slurs, CRT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that record stories of racism, include racial slurs, are perceived as teaching 'Critical Race Theory', or are ambiguous on race issues are often targeted for censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges may arise from discomfort with historical language or portrayals; defenders argue such works provide historically-accurate or anti-racist perspectives and have educational value. Claims of 'CRT' are sometimes used as a catch-all to oppose race- or equity-related content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social grounds (moral/social character concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Books suppressed because of language, racial characterization, depiction of drug use, social class, sexual orientation, or other social differences that challengers view as harmful to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censors may argue rebellious characters or anti-authoritarian themes will negatively influence youth; opponents argue such themes have literary merit and can foster critical thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political grounds for suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Books have been suppressed for political content perceived as promoting anarchism, communism, socialism, or otherwise politically objectionable viewpoints; suppression can also be instigated by foreign governments (e.g., China Lobby case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples include widespread restriction during the Red Scare; political suppression can come from local governments, school districts, or external pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious grounds for challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are challenged when content is seen to attack or conflict with particular religious beliefs, or to promote witchcraft/occult practices (e.g., evolution or fantasy works like Harry Potter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious objections may lead to removals or curricular exclusions; courts and policies sometimes weigh religious objections against academic freedom and First Amendment considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security / national-security-based censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Government actors have attempted to censor books on the basis that they disclose sensitive information or threaten security (e.g., Operation Dark Heart; CIA censorship of classified or sensitive material).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such censorship may involve prepublication review or redaction, and can raise distinct legal and policy issues compared with school/library challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental control and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to challenges sometimes include parental-permission policies, offering alternatives to challenged books, or policies that give parents increased control over what children may read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may require parental permission to access certain titles or offer alternate assignments; these measures are used as compromises but can also be criticized as constraining students' access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redaction as a remediation / censoring technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Redaction involves striking through or covering sections of materials so they cannot be seen by readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a way to make specific passages inaccessible while leaving the rest of the work available; raises questions about integrity of the work and pedagogical efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional actors and challengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities requesting censorship may include organizations, private individuals, or government officials; institutional decision-makers include school boards, administrators, librarians, library committees, and reconsideration committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding who initiates and who decides is crucial to analyzing process, accountability, and the legitimacy of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of centralized reporting and data (especially prisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often a lack of centralized data and mandatory reporting about censored titles (notably in federal prisons), making it difficult to quantify and analyze the full scope of censorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of reporting requirements hampers oversight and public understanding; advocacy groups like PEN and ALA collect and publish incident-based data to fill gaps.
